Problem BreachLock is solving

* **No clear view of attack surface**
  
  * Companies don’t know all exposed assets (cloud, APIs, shadow IT, vendors)
  
  * External + internal exposure constantly changing
* **Pentesting is outdated**
  
  * Annual / quarterly → quickly becomes irrelevant
  
  * Expensive, manual, slow turnaround
* **Too many fragmented tools**
  
  * Separate tools for scanning, ASM, pentesting, reporting
  
  * No unified view → poor prioritization
* **Signal vs noise problem**
  
  * Too many vulnerabilities, unclear which are exploitable
  
  * Security teams struggle to prioritize fixes

Patero is a **network and communications security platform** focused on **quantum-safe encryption** and **zero-trust remote access**.



In practice, it helps enterprises protect data in transit by cloaking internet-exposed endpoints, reducing attack surface, and encrypting traffic with a mix of classical and post-quantum cryptography. It also offers **cryptographic inventory / quantum-readiness assessment**, so companies can identify where they rely on legacy encryption and plan migration to post-quantum standards.



Their positioning is strongest around critical infrastructure, federal, and defense-oriented environments.



**Patero cloaks exposed network endpoints - making it difficult for cyber terrorists to find points of attack. Data is \"double encrypted\" with classic and post-quantum encryption keys.**

Tumeryk is an **AI security and governance layer for GenAI applications, LLMs, and AI agents**. Its core offering includes **real-time trust scoring**, **guardrails**, **red teaming**, and **observability** for AI systems.



That means it helps enterprises test models for things like jailbreaks, hallucinations, prompt injection, bias, and data leakage; enforce policies on prompts and outputs; and continuously monitor how models behave in production



In Short:  
Tumeryk is like a **security + control plane for enterprise AI apps**—it makes sure GenAI systems are **safe, policy-compliant, and production-ready**.

Intro: Rao Cherukuri <> Ravish, DVC

Thu, 19 Mar 26

Ravish

* Connected to Sundar through IIT Madras network
  
  * Previously helped Sundar with VC introductions during ideation phase
  
  * Reconnected when Sundar officially launched Agent ID

Agent ID Investment Context

* Rao invested in Agent ID’s pre-seed round

* Also includes investment from Arali (not as incubator, straight safe)

* Rao’s expertise in cloud security/identity management drove investment thesis
  
  * Background includes identity, access control, tokenization
  
  * Sees AI identity management as much bigger problem than current human-focused infrastructure
* Agent ID approach: Just-in-time access control for dynamic AI agent environments
  
  * Easy insertion point - no need to change existing infrastructure
  
  * Runtime policy enforcement based on intent

Founder Assessment - Sundar

* Third-time founder with two previous exits

* Strong technical understanding of runtime access control

* Good at solving complex problems at scale

* Single founder (no co-founder plans despite suggestions)

* Building team primarily in India while based in Bay Area

Investment Concerns & Red Flags

* Dual US/India structure complicating fundraising
  
  * Been working on legal structure for couple months
  
  * Will make next round difficult for US investors
  
  * Sundar unwilling to change structure despite feedback
* Crowded market with many companies tackling AI identity management
  
  * Risk that established IAM players could add as feature
  
  * Betting more on founder execution than unique approach
* Fundraising approach lacks systematic strategy
  
  * Should focus on clean Bay Area raise given location and capital availability
  
  
Next Steps

* Rao offered to help with market insights and connections

* Acknowledged honest feedback exchange valuable for both parties

* No specific follow-up actions defined

* * *

Sundar’s Background & Previous Exits

* Two successful exits in cybersecurity space
  
  * Wagum (2013-2017): Industrial IoT mobile platform, raised $4M, sold for $17M to Rockwell/Johnson Controls
  
  * Scan AI (recent): DevSecOps company, raised ~$1M from angels, acquired by Fortinet for $13M
    
    * Product became FortiDevSec, grew to $20M revenue
    
    * Also managed FortiWeb (WAF product) from $65M to $100M
* Currently based in Las Vegas, fund team mostly in Dallas

Agntid Funding & Structure

* Raised $500K from cybersecurity founder angels (6-7 investors)
  
  * Includes Kano, Tanu Kulati (Austin-based), Securonics founder
  
  * Signed term sheet with Arali Ventures (India VC)
  
  * $1M investment into $2M round at $10M post-money cap
  
  * CCD structure (similar to SAFE) with put/call conversion mechanism
  
  * Requires India company incorporation due to CTO location
  
  * Term sheet signed December, still working through definitive docs
* Considering additional investors but capping round at $2M to limit dilution

Product & Market Position

* AI agent authorization/access control platform
  
  * Focus on enforcement layer vs traditional IAM authentication
  
  * MCP (Model Control Protocol) proxy architecture
  
  * Customer-hosted runtime, no cloud dependency
* Target customers: Infrastructure/IAM teams at medium-large enterprises
  
  * Need separate IAM and security teams to understand the problem
  
  * Centralized governance across multiple dev teams using different AI frameworks
* Current traction: Design partners including Cisco (two separate use cases), ThousandEyes, Vanguard

Competitive Landscape Analysis

* Differentiated from tool-calling platforms (Arcade) which became less relevant post-MCP standardization

* Distinct from policy engines ([Permit.io][1]) focused on developer-centric approaches

* Different from workload identity platforms (Ambient) targeting infrastructure security

* Positioned as new category within identity (IAM/IGA space)
  
  * IAM (Okta): Authentication and token issuance
  
  * IGA (SailPoint): Governance and compliance
  
  * Tinitusk: Real-time enforcement in execution path

Next Steps

* Sundar to send pitch deck to Ravish

* Ravish to discuss internally with US and India partners
  
  * Determine if investment timing aligns (normally too early stage)
  
  * Decide US vs India fund structure (US preferred for simplicity)
  
  * Potentially involve technical advisor for deeper product evaluation
* Follow-up call planned for next week if internal interest confirmed

**Core Concern: AI Liability in Audit**

* Biggest blocker to adoption is legal/professional risk, not capability
  
  * If AI produces an output and the audit fails, “we put it in the machine and it spat out an answer” is not a defensible position in litigation
  
  * Enron/Andersen cited as the stakes: one bad audit can destroy a firm
* Traceability features don’t fully resolve the risk
  
  * Re-performing what the AI did to verify it eliminates the efficiency gain
  
  * Prompt testing and accuracy validation (which Talon is doing) seen as critical but not yet sufficient
  
  * Auditors will still need to exercise judgment on outputs — trust hasn’t been established legally
  
  
**Where AI Actually Fits in Audit Workflows**

* Hard part of audit is judgment, risk assessment, and project management — not procedure execution
  
  * Missing a deadline can get you fired even if the accounting is perfect
  
  * Ryan’s current AI focus: admin and project management tasks (low-risk, high-efficiency)
  
  * Scheduling, client follow-ups, timeline management — no liability exposure
  
  * Existing audit software (e.g., Caseware) is basic workflow tooling, not intelligent

* Data Snipper example: Excel add-on that links source docs to data — 90% faster for confirmations
  
  * Illustrates appetite for targeted, low-risk efficiency tools
  
  
**Adoption Dynamics at Large Firms**

* Even if Baker Tilly commits, rollout would be cautious
  
  * ~20 pilot engagements across industry groups, run side-by-side with normal audits
  
  * Firm-wide mandate unlikely; individual partners/principals hard to force
* Cultural resistance is real — Ryan has seen many firm-wide initiatives quietly abandoned when 85–90% of staff don’t comply

* Competitive pressure may be the forcing function

Guard0 meeting notes (Feb 11, Dallas VC call)

1) What Guard0 is building

Guard0 is positioning as an **AI security + governance platform** that sits across the enterprise’s AI stack (apps, agents, models, tools, data) and answers two urgent buyer needs:

* **“What do we have?”** Full **AI/agent inventory + asset graph** across code + cloud + agent platforms.

* **“What can go wrong?”** **Context-aware, non-deterministic security testing** (dynamic attacks) for AI apps and agents.

* **“How do we operationalize controls?”** **Governance + workflows** integrated into agent platforms and developer/AppSec tooling.

They explicitly dislike “AI AppSec = old AppSec policies relabeled for AI” and claim their core advantage is **dynamic testing driven by business context**, not deterministic policy checks.

* * *

2) Founder background (as stated)

* Founder spent ~6 years building API security / posture management (mentions acquisition; likely referencing Traceable AI experience).

* Early career includes hands-on product + GTM + customer success in an early-stage context.

* MS from Stanford University.

* Last ~8 months focused full-time on Guard0 (product came from customer discovery in 2024–2025, especially regulated enterprises).

* * *

3) Product pillars (how they describe it)

Pillar A: AI + Agent discovery (inventory)

Goal: give CISOs/CSOs visibility without slowing engineering.

* Data sources: “code + cloud sync” (implies deep integration into CI/CD + cloud control plane + logs; they explicitly mention visibility across Microsoft Azure / Google Cloud / AWS signals).

* Output: “95%+ AI landscape” view: AI apps, models, prompts, tool access, DB access, MCPs, agent platform usage, and activity.

**Why it resonates:** Security leaders want to avoid being blindsided later (“if something goes wrong in 6 months”), but engineering doesn’t want security gating adoption.

Pillar B: Dynamic attacks (AI security testing with context)

They claim they can generate **business-logic-specific attack payloads** using context inferred from the environment.



Example they gave:



* Detect system prompt uses **user input**.

* Check for input validation / guardrails.

* Attempt payload injection and measure impact based on access scope (data sensitivity, tool access).

* Produce evidence trail: chat transcript, data flow, code location, and suggested fix.

This is framed as materially better than “prompt injection scanners” that don’t understand app context.

Pillar C: Agent platform governance layer

This is the “platform” angle: integrate with agent platforms to provide a centralized view and controls:

* For each agent: tool permissions, data access, executed actions, behavioral baselines.

* Detect over-privilege (example: agent has write access to Salesforce but should be read-only).

* Provide compliance/posture reporting for leadership and board-level reporting.

They cited specific conversations with large orgs and agent-platform initiatives, including Roblox and JPMorgan Chase (and also referenced Bank of America, American Express, LinkedIn, Intuit).

* * *

4) Differentiation claim (their words, normalized)

1.  **No “heavy proxy/VPN” deployment**: they suggest alternatives rely on heavyweight inline controls (proxy/VPN) that hurt adoption.

2.  **Fast onboarding**: connect to code + cloud + agent platforms, get “first 90%” quickly.

3.  **Context-driven security efficacy**: they quoted **~85–90% efficacy** for their dynamic attacks (note: this needs validation; “efficacy” definition is unclear: precision/recall? exploit success? true-positive rate?).

* * *

5) ICP, buyer, and user (important nuance)

* **Economic buyer:** usually **CISO/CSO** or **CIO** (depends on org and whether it’s framed as security vs platform governance).

* **Primary users/workflows:** **AppSec + developers** (ticketing, fixes, Slack/engineering workflows).

* **Secondary consumers:** security leadership (reports, posture scores, board reporting templates).

This matters because Guard0 is trying to be both:

* A security leader visibility + governance system, and

* A developer/AppSec workflow engine that drives remediation.

* * *

6) Adoption psychology (what’s driving urgency)

Their strongest “why now” narrative is not “agents are scary,” it’s:

* Enterprises already have **hundreds of AI apps** (they cited one bank with ~340 AI apps by H1 2025; 80% prod).

* Board + competitive pressure is accelerating AI deployment.

* Engineering wants speed; security fears blind spots.

* Therefore, the wedge is **visibility without friction**, then expand into testing + governance.

* * *

7) GTM motion (as implied)

* Starts with POV/POC to prove discovery coverage + value quickly.

* Sells into large enterprises where platform expectation exists: land with one module, expand into platform.

They explicitly said SMBs may buy point products, but large enterprises will eventually push for a broader platform.

**/Market Segmentation and Challenges**

Primary Focus: Generating invoices and accepting digital payments.

Common Solutions: Lightweight tools integrated with QuickBooks, Xero, Zoho Books, etc. Examples include Bill.com, Invoice2go, etc.

Challenges: Transition from simple invoicing to handling various customer types, payment methods, terms, and invoicing models.



**Why Mid-Market Companies?**

Managing more complex invoicing and payment processes, integrating with ERP systems like NetSuite, Sage, Microsoft Dynamics.

Sometimes use ERP for invoicing or specialized billing systems like Chargebee or Zuora for subscriptions.

Challenges: Complex workflows from quote to invoicing, handling various business models (transactional, subscription, usage-based, services, contract-based), and integrating multiple payment and invoicing systems.



**Other players vs Growfin**

Custom-built solutions on top of robust ERPs (SAP, Oracle) with help from large service providers (Infosys, TCS, Accenture).

High Radius, GetPaid, etc., which integrate deeply with ERP systems.

Challenges: Long implementation cycles, high complexity, and the need for highly customized solutions.



**/Workflow Complexity and Stakeholders**

Different payment methods, currencies, banks, and delivery systems increase complexity.

Involvement of finance, sales, and customer success teams. Sales commissions often tied to collections, necessitating their involvement.

Real-time data syncing across different systems and stakeholders, maintaining context for all parties involved.



**/Key Integrations and Data Sources**

CRM and ERP Systems: Integration with CRM (like Salesforce) and ERP (like NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365).

Integration with email, Slack, Microsoft Teams for streamlined communication.

Bank and Payment Gateways: Pulling transaction data from banks and processing payments through gateways.

Using AI to match payments to invoices, handling various formats of remittance advice (emails, PDFs, etc.), and reconciling with ERP.



**/Differentiation and Competitive Landscape**

Offering end-to-end automation for collections, payments, and cash application.

Ease of Implementation: Quick, plug-and-play integrations with existing tech stacks, avoiding long implementation cycles.

Customer Relationship Focus: Emphasizing the importance of customer relationships in collections, not just automation.

Competitors: Tesorio, Versapay, YayPay, High Radius (in some mid-market deals), and other automation-focused providers.

Addressing Manual Processes and Partner Channels

Current way: Mostly companies relying on manual processes and spreadsheets.

Potential partnerships with ERP providers as go-to-market channels, leveraging their ecosystems.

* **General Philosophy on Introductions**:
  
  * DVC typically makes introductions for companies even if not planning to invest, as part of building a long-term reputation and goodwill.
  
  * Introductions are limited to warm intros and feedback requests, not extensive support like with portfolio companies.
* **Phoenix Security - Current Assessment**:
  
  * Their product addressing vulnerability prioritization is valuable and addresses a key market pain point.
  
  * Two conditions for DVC investment:
    
    1.  Phoenix remains a UK company and aligns the investment structure.
    
    2.  Phoenix flips/re-domiciles to the US (with significant costs and risks for both parties).
* **Challenges with US Market Entry**:
  
  * Flipping to the US would cost ~$30K–$100K and require significant legal, tax, and operational efforts, which Phoenix may not be ready for given its current financials and traction.
  
  * Francesco might prioritize building traction in the EU and Nordics while gradually chipping away at the US pipeline.
  
  * A direct GTM setup in the US is too resource-intensive for Phoenix at its current stage.
* **Alternative Suggestions**:
  
  * Introduce Francesco to US GTM/sales agency firms to help build traction in a cost-effective and lower-risk manner.
  
  * Focus on strengthening Phoenix’s EU and US pipelines, refining the product, and shoring up the engineering team to handle multiple time zones.
* **Next Steps**:
  
  * Francesco will reassess after closing his next funding round and gaining more traction.
  
  * DVC will re-engage later, depending on the evolution of the product, market, and Phoenix’s willingness to meet the above conditions.
  
  * Meanwhile, targeted introductions to friendly CISOs or customers can provide feedback without overcommitting time or resources.

  * Maintain engagement with Phoenix through discussions, introductions, and incremental steps while waiting for clarity on their strategic direction.

**Product & Technology Differentiators**

* **Platform Focus & Unique Selling Propositions (USPs):**
  
  * Phoenix focuses on comprehensive vulnerability management with a strong emphasis on contextual prioritization and deduplication, aiming to minimize \"vulnerability noise.\"
  
  * The solution provides actionable risk prioritization across cloud, container, and application layers, allowing seamless correlation from code to cloud.
* **Key Features:**
  
  * **Contextual Deduplication:** Distinguishes between vulnerabilities that need immediate attention vs. those that don’t, reducing vulnerability clutter.
  
  * **Risk & Impact Scoring:** Uses a four-dimensional risk model (including EPSS and external/internal exposure) to create a nuanced view of vulnerabilities.
  
  * **Real-time Insights and Board-Level Reporting:** Allows for real-time monitoring, board-level insights on vulnerability resolution, and risk reduction reporting.
* **Integrations & Compatibility:**
  
  * Natively integrates with GitHub, CICD pipelines, AWS, Azure, and key security tools (e.g., Qualys, Snyk).
  
  * Differentiates itself from Vulcan, Nucleus, and Armor Code by focusing on deep contextual analysis over mere vulnerability aggregation.

**Go-To-Market (GTM) Strategy**

* **Target Market & Initial Penetration:**
  
  * Initially targeting FinTech and financial institutions, with expansion in North America and European markets.
  
  * Directly approaching organizations with 1,000–3,000 developers, aiming to expand within each client by addressing cloud, app, and operational security layers.
* **Sales Motion:**
  
  * Relationship-driven strategy involving executive dinners, networking events, and leveraging existing clients as case studies for growth in specific U.S. hubs (e.g., North Carolina, Texas).
  
  * Lean team currently with one Account Executive (AE) in the U.S., with plans to double down on U.S. hires and establish regional hubs.
* **Competitive Landscape:**
  
  * Competes with tools like Vulcan and Nucleus on vulnerability management but emphasizes unique aspects of contextual prioritization and deduplication.
  
  * Partners with Anika and other scanning-focused platforms for complementary solutions.

**Sales & Revenue Model**

* **Current Performance & Key Metrics:**
  
  * Current ARR at $610,000, with a goal of reaching $1.2M–1.4M by year-end, marking significant growth.
  
  * Expansion strategy with clients involves cross-selling to additional application, cloud, or operational security use cases.
* **Pricing Structure:**
  
  * Current model is asset-based, allowing for clear scaling with client growth, though the team is refining this to reduce sales friction and improve simplicity.
  
  * Average Contract Value (ACV) is approximately $150K–200K, with larger enterprise deals reaching $500K+.
* **Expansion Dynamics:**
  
  * Expands within accounts based on asset growth, broadening to different security layers or scaling usage in larger enterprises.
  
  * Current clients include key logos in finance and FinTech, with steady growth in recurring revenue.

**Funding & Growth Plans**

* **Funding Details:**
  
  * Phoenix has raised $5M, with a 2-year runway supporting targeted growth initiatives in the U.S.
  
  * Seeking a U.S.-based co-lead for Series A to enhance domestic presence and market penetration, aiming for alignment with an investor familiar with cybersecurity and the evolving U.S. regulatory landscape.
* **Expansion Strategy:**
  
  * Francesco plans to relocate to the U.S. for closer customer engagement and GTM leadership, establishing Phoenix’s U.S. headquarters in either Texas or Boston.
  
  * Engineering and product teams remain Europe-based, led by co-founder Alfonso, allowing Francesco to fully focus on sales and growth in North America.
* **Long-term Vision:**
  
  * The team envisions expanding their platform capabilities to support broader DevSecOps functions, increasing automation in asset mapping, and creating further integration with IT asset management and application performance management tools.
  
  
**Next Steps and DVC’s Perspective**

* **DVC’s Considerations:**
  
  * Dallas Venture Capital expressed interest in Phoenix Security’s solution and market approach but needs further internal discussion to determine if current metrics warrant investment at this stage.
  
  * Key concerns include Phoenix’s revenue maturity ($610K ARR) and limited U.S. presence, with the team weighing the option to either join this round or wait for Phoenix’s next round.

If you happen to revisit the recording of the meeting, you will probably get most of these, but just wanted to bring out a few things that stood out in my mind.

* Although Jay mentioned, 30% of revenue is from Drive-Thru, neither the deck nor during the conversation, he brought any of the known brand names. As my focus was not on delving deeper into the business side of the conversation, I purposefully avoided asking for any specific brand / client names. Please refer to the attached for some deeper insights on the Drive-Thru trends from the market. As you can see, the Voice AI based ordering is still in its Day 0.

* I felt he avoided sharing details around the Edge hardware - which they refer as VoicePod. He just said, it can be easily installed by the brand\'s themselves because the already have cracked the integration with known Drive-Thru equipment brands - HME etc. That is why they can bring a system up and running in 10-12 weeks timeframe. During this time, they also capture data for the brand that they use to train a custom model as well. The domain is price sensitive in every step of the way, so additional hardware / installation etc., create some element of friction / hurdle to overcome to scale - any edge device will mean - an elaborate set of infrastructure to monitor the health of the device, upgrade software, cybersecurity needs etc., as well. That is a challenge, we didn\'t delve much deeper on as the focus was understanding the solution

* Patent provides good defensibility, but others are arming their warchest to defend their turf. He did bring up the company names like Valyant, but not in a lot of detail though. My research makes me believe Valyant\'s acquisition by ConverseNow was to arm themselves more with more patents / definisiblity or even prepare themselves for future M&A. - [Links to some Valyant AI patents here][2].

* There were some very valid arguments about apparent failures that industry has encountered and still recovering from those failed experiments - McD\'s - Israeli startup acquisition -> Sale to IBM and eventually halting the collaborative effort with them completely is one. The other he did bring up is Google\'s apparent failed ongoing experiments with Wendy\'s

* We spent about 60-70% of the time talking about Phone based solution - which is primarily Twilio / CTI, Azure / Nuance ASR and custom dialog management and custom built model for the brand\'s respective products / offerings. This seems the most common format and I did bring up YC company. His counter was that there are far too many companies, but no one has the contextual data and custom model with 95%+ accuracy in the market and that is how he differentiates from the rest of the competition

* Pizzavoice seems to be a unique offering and I requested him for either a access to a Sandbox to playaround or calling a nearby location which has Voiceplug solution live. Yet to receive anything as yet, but just wanted to bring it up here.

There are a couple companies that have gone on to raise their Series A in this domain - ConverseNow, Hi.auto, OpenCity etc., but to me none of them have any major commercialization breakthrough as yet. So if smaller regional brands are open to adapt the solution, explore and exploit the tech\' solution superiority, then this could be game changing.

They emphasized the fact that they have both extension and browser which help them serve both employees(who would prefer extension) and BYOD type users (that require actual browser).

Both are required to be good for enterprise browser to penetrate into the market well. Based on the call, I felt that they have focused a lot of more on DLP. They demonstrated numerous controls that are available to control the data/document flow for the end user. The number of controls they implemented is somewhat overwhelming for the admins. It gave me a feeling that they kept adding controls as customers kept asking more. This practice would be good if the company has a product strategy that they followed but it felt more like the features were driven by various customers that asked features for their specific needs.

Surf Tech team also emphasized the fact that they have a chrome extension that supports the exact same features as their enterprise browser. Extension would make it much easier to roll out the product to enterprise users that already have company managed devices. However, on company managed devices, there are many other competitive options available to control the data and implement DLP. Enterprises have policies that are different when users are on company networks vs third party networks. Many of the access policies are directly managed at network level (Through firewall, proxy, SASE etc). Also, DLP on an enterprise managed device needs to cover other apps too (like Teams, Outlook etc). In that sense, having an extensive set of DLP features just for browser (extension) may not make it more appealing for enterprise customers to deploy this solution on corporate managed devices.

On the network side, Surf Tech claims their product is much better than their competitors. But I didn\'t see how. The only option for customers to access their assets behind the firewall, is to deploy a proxy inside their firewall to use this product. I am not convinced that this option will work for many customers. They didn\'t seem to put a lot of focus into corporate network side of integration.

In summary, I think this product may work (or may be designed) for MSPs or small enterprises. But in its current shape, it may not compete well with the segment that Island and Talon target. If they want to target bigger enterprises, they need help on product strategy and a GTM strategy to align with it.

Notes:

Tinybird is solving customer\'s \"data extraction and ingestion\" problems by building data pipelines, enabling real-time and user-facing analytics.

1) There are dozens of companies doing what they are doing. In fact, Tinybird does not have any unique technology. advantage or patents in this area/

2) They have limited connectors. Companies like Syncsort, Informatica, or other startups have hundreds of connectors to extract data in real time from source systems.

3) Tinybird has not mentioned whether it is using AI or GenAI technologies to build efficient data pipelines. While building pipelines customers need to validate the data, improve the data quality, etc. They have not mentioned if they have built-in technology to improve data quality. For example if we are extracting customer information we need to make sure the address, zip code, state, country, phone number, etc are valid.

4) The reviews on AWS marketplace are not great.[ https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/reviews/reviews-list/prodview-u264uwpaelwmq][1]

5) Since it is a SaaS product, it will not be adopted in regulatory spaces like financials and healthcare. Regulated industries typically do not allow the data to leave their network. In cases where customers approve the SaaS product, the bar is very high and the company must have a compelling product.

6) Most of the companies they mention as having customers might be small companies. This in itself is not bad but increasing adoption (and revenues) in small companies takes time. THe support costs with smaller companies will be higher per $1M dollars in revenue.

7) Tinybird claims to be a managed version of Clickhouse ([https://clickhouse.com/clickhouse][2]). It seems like Clickhouse is an open-source version. I don\'t know the differences between Clickhouse and Tineybird, and potential customers will be willing to pay for Tiny Bird.

8) Tinybird might be a good option for a startup that only needs data to be extracted from the sources Tinybird supports.

9) If we have access to the Tinybird investors deck we can see their product and business development plans, which will help us evaluate them.

At the end of the day, I don\'t see any compelling reason why enterprise customers might want to use them.

**Feedback from Raghuveer:**



**Based on our call with Surf Tech, here is my feedback:**

The team is good with strong technical background. They seem comfortable with Chromium which is a critical piece for this solution to work. They have a lot of features and the product is working well. They emphasized the fact that they have both extension and browser which help them serve both employees(who would prefer extension) and BYOD type users (that require actual browser).

Typically, enterprise browsers have 2 areas of focus. 1) Secure access to enterprise assets 2) DLP (Data Loss Prevention). Both are required to be good for enterprise browser to penetrate into the market well. Based on the call, I felt that they have focused a lot of more on DLP. They demonstrated numerous controls that are available to control the data/document flow for the end user. The number of controls they implemented is somewhat overwhelming for the admins. It gave me a feeling that they kept adding controls as customers kept asking more. This practice would be good if the company has a product strategy that they followed but it felt more like the features were driven by various customers that asked features for their specific needs.

Surf Tech team also emphasized the fact that they have a chrome extension that supports the exact same features as their enterprise browser. Extension would make it much easier to roll out the product to enterprise users that already have company managed devices. However, on company managed devices, there are many other competitive options available to control the data and implement DLP. Enterprises have policies that are different when users are on company networks vs third party networks. Many of the access policies are directly managed at network level (Through firewall, proxy, SASE etc). Also, DLP on an enterprise managed device needs to cover other apps too (like Teams, Outlook etc). In that sense, having an extensive set of DLP features just for browser (extension) may not make it more appealing for enterprise customers to deploy this solution on corporate managed devices.

On the network side, Surf Tech claims their product is much better than their competitors. But I didn\'t see how. The only option for customers to access their assets behind the firewall, is to deploy a proxy inside their firewall to use this product. I am not convinced that this option will work for many customers. They didn\'t seem to put a lot of focus into corporate network side of integration.

In summary, I think this product may work (or may be designed) for MSPs or small enterprises. But in its current shape, it may not compete well with the segment that Island and Talon target. If they want to target bigger enterprises, they need help on product strategy and a GTM strategy to align with it.

\- **Product Use Cases:**

\- Secures managed devices from web threats, including DNS filtering, web categorization, and secure web access gateways.

* **Ballerine’s Positioning**: Ravish’s firm, primarily focused on enterprise software rather than niche fintech areas, views Ballerine as an infrastructure provider for KYC processes rather than a traditional payments solution.

* **Aneliya’s Experience and Context**: With a decade at Nuvei, Aneliya shared insights from her global experience in underwriting and KYC. She described the market demand for streamlined, compliant onboarding and the existing gaps in many KYC systems.

* **Ballerine’s Strengths**:
  
  * **Comprehensive Coverage**: Ballerine covers a broad array of KYC checks, including onboarding, ongoing, and post-boarding monitoring.
  
  * **Flexibility and Customization**: The platform can be customized for geographic and regulatory needs, with robust API integrations, including CRM connectivity—something most competitors lack.
  
  * **Partnership Approach**: Ballerine’s responsive and collaborative team listens to client needs, positioning them as more than just a vendor.
* **Competitors and Market Gaps**: Competitors like Infinicept and Dun & Bradstreet only partially meet KYC needs. Ballerine stands out for its full end-to-end onboarding capabilities.

* **Expansion Potential**: Ravish explored the potential for Ballerine beyond fintech, with possible applications in e-commerce and lending, where KYC is also essential. Aneliya agreed, noting Ballerine’s scalability for other sectors with KYC needs.

* **Areas for Improvement**: Aneliya suggested that Ballerine could benefit from more visual presentations and mockups to help non-technical users understand the platform.

* **Positive Outlook**: Both Ravish and Aneliya expressed confidence in Ballerine’s potential. Ravish emphasized his firm’s enthusiasm, and Aneliya noted her belief in Ballerine’s alignment with market needs and its adaptability to evolving KYC demands.

Ballerine is focused on building a scalable and developer-centric risk infrastructure to help clients onboard, underwrite, and monitor customers effectively. Initially launched as an open-source platform, Ballerine aimed to tackle the fragmented data sources and tools available in the market, providing a flexible infrastructure to support various use cases. They launched a SaaS offering and, despite early-stage status, onboarded enterprise clients with high potential value, emphasizing a merchant acquiring focus.

**Summary of Key Points:**

1.  **Flexible Risk Infrastructure:** Ballerine provides a modular and scalable risk management solution, initially launched as an open-source project to cater to diverse clients and learn from multiple use cases.

2.  **Product Evolution and Focus:** The company is focusing on merchant acquiring as its initial commercial application, leveraging its infrastructure for underwriting, KYB (Know Your Business), and ongoing monitoring of merchants. The product integrates various data sources and offers a streamlined platform for clients.

3.  **Partnerships and Certification:** Ballerine has become a Mastercard-certified compliance partner, providing acquirers up to 75% fine discounts when utilizing their platform. They also collaborate with Visa and are exploring additional commercial and technical partnerships through Mastercard’s acceleration program.

4.  **Global Expansion and GTM Strategy:** The company has hired key personnel in Singapore and Hong Kong to capitalize on opportunities in APAC. Ballerine is expanding its go-to-market (GTM) efforts in these regions to capture the demand for risk management solutions tailored to local regulations and merchant requirements.

5.  **Revenue Model:** Ballerine charges platform fees and usage fees based on client needs (e.g., registry data, KYC, ID verification). Clients are billed annually based on packages, providing predictable revenue streams. The pricing structure typically results in fees of around $30 per merchant onboarded and additional charges for compliance monitoring and web presence analysis.

6.  **Future Growth Plans:** Ballerine plans to introduce new products like AI-assisted analysis tools and a self-serve platform for broader industry use cases. The company is also considering expanding its database services for fraud detection and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) storage as part of its network effect strategy.

7.  **Funding and Financials:** After participating in Y Combinator and raising $5 million from investors like Dimit Capital, Veri Equity, and fintech angel investors, Ballerine has about $2 million remaining in the bank. The company is deciding between raising additional funds through a $5 million SAFE round or a larger $10 million priced round, aiming for a valuation range of $20-$30 million pre-money.

8.  **Target Clients and Use Cases:** The primary focus remains on merchant acquirers in the e-commerce space. However, the infrastructure is adaptable for other industries, including lending, insurance, and business banking, indicating potential for diversified growth.

Ballerine\'s approach combines flexibility, scalability, and modularity, making it well-positioned to address evolving risk management challenges for acquirers and PSPs (Payment Service Providers). The company\'s strong industry partnerships, especially with Mastercard, underscore its credibility and future potential for scaling its business.

* Their observability platform allows users to monitor and analyze AI model performance in real-time, enabling proactive intervention and decision-making.

* The security aspect involves ensuring compliance, data protection, and mitigating risks associated with AI model outputs, such as toxic responses or privacy violations.

* WhyLabs stands out for being a SaaS platform, catering to enterprises with production-grade AI workloads as opposed to competitors like Arize.

**Call with Rahul, Kalyan, and Ravish:**



**Fund Flexibility and Investment Considerations:**

* A US presence is preferred for investments from the US fund, but it\'s not mandatory. The company’s future plans, current market focus, and incorporation location play crucial roles in deciding the


**Company Incorporation and Market Presence:**

* The company is incorporated in Singapore.

* Currently, 70% of its customers and revenue come from India, with 30% from international markets, mostly the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region and some from the Western Hemisphere.

* Most customers in India are large enterprises.

**Challenges and Strategic Growth Needs:**

* The company has faced challenges with global growth due to the structure of past funding, which has primarily flowed into the Indian entity, limiting growth in international markets.


They aim to raise funds outside India to support global expansion, particularly in markets like the US and UK.

**Team Backgrounds and Company History:**

* Kalyan - The finance lead is a qualified chartered accountant and company secretary with 12+ years in startups, experienced in M&A, acqui-hires, and financing rounds.

* Rahul - The founder has a strong background in cybersecurity, dropping out of college to work in the field and later starting the company in 2015. The company bootstrapped for three years before raising external funding.

* They replaced the external CEO hired in 2019 due to a mismatch in sales approach and took back control, significantly growing ARR since then.

**Product Overview and Differentiation:**

* The company focuses on cybersecurity intelligence rather than network security or traditional software supply chain monitoring.

* It offers a comprehensive platform that integrates various monitoring solutions (e.g., vendor security, dark web, attack surface) into a single pane of glass.

* Differentiates itself from competitors like Palo Alto by focusing on external threats and providing actionable intelligence, rather than just internal threat monitoring.

**GTM Strategy:**

* The company has three GTM strategies:

* \- **Bullwhip Effect:** Existing customers, such as large banks, use the product to monitor their vendors and subsidiaries, which leads those entities to adopt the product themselves.

* \- **Partnerships:** Over 30% of their revenue comes from partnerships, especially in the Middle East. Partners are incentivized with a 15% revenue share.

* \- **Free Tool (Bayvigil):** A community tool to generate leads by providing free security scores and threat intelligence, leading to conversions for the enterprise product.

* \- The company does not plan to invest in a direct sales team for the US market but will focus on channel partnerships.

**Team Composition and Structure:**

* Total headcount is approximately 200.

* The split includes around 80 in product engineering and research, 20 in customer services, 30 in sales, 18 in marketing (including BDRs), and 20 in corporate functions.

* The majority of the team is based in Bangalore, India, with a few exceptions.

**Financials and Funding Round:**

* The company is looking to raise $20 million in a new round.

* The raised funds will be used to grow the customer base from 10 to 100 in regions like the US and UK through partnerships rather than direct sales.

* India is a profitable market, and the company aims to grow its customer base from 120 to 400 in India.

* Existing investors are expected to participate in this round, and there is already a non-lead term sheet with a valuation provided by an investor.

**Churn and Customer Retention:**

* Net Revenue Retention (NRR) is 104%, with a trailing 12-month data showing revenue churn of 9-10%.

* Churn reasons include false positives, false negatives, and price sensitivity among smaller clients. The company tries to push SMB clients to upgrade or churn them if they remain small accounts.

**Future Plans:**

* The company plans to grow to $50 million ARR in the next few years and aims to become a prominent cybersecurity company in India and potentially go public.

* It is focusing on maintaining cost efficiency and investing heavily in engineering and R&D while expanding strategically in global markets.

**Overview:**

* There are two kinds of SaaS companies regarding integration:
  
  1.  Large companies offering integration services via system integrators/professional services.
  
  2.  Smaller companies integrating at the product feature level early in development.
* SaaS developers face the challenge of building and maintaining many integrations (e.g., CRM systems like Salesforce, and HubSpot), which is time-consuming and requires continuous maintenance.

**Current Approaches:**

1.  **In-house integrations:** Developers need to manually read API documentation, handle rate limits, and transform data models, often taking 4-6 weeks for a single integration.

2.  **Third-party tools (e.g., Zapier):** Customers buy additional tools for integrations, but they often prefer integration to be part of the product.

3.  **Unified APIs & Embedded Workflow Solutions:**
    
    * **Unified APIs:** Standardize various SaaS tools into a common API (e.g., Merge.dev for CRM). This simplifies integration for developers but leaves out many use cases.
    
    * **Embedded Workflows/IPaaS:** Offers orchestration tools for custom business logic via drag-and-drop but requires developers to learn specific APIs for every new integration.

**Challenges with Current Solutions:**

* Unified APIs struggle with scaling API coverage, leaving many customer use cases unsolved.

* Embedded tools offer better API coverage but force developers to learn each system’s API.

**Knit.dev Solution:**

* **Agent-based integration:** Uses an AI-driven multi-agent system. One agent scrapes API documentation and converts APIs into executable code units stored in a vector database. Another agent interacts with developers, providing custom connectors that don’t require understanding the source API.

* Offers 100% API coverage by scraping API documentation and automating much of the developer effort.

* Reduced integration development time from 4-6 weeks to 2 days, positioning the company for faster catalog expansion.

**Business Traction:**

* Knit.dev has 20 customers, with 50% in North America (NA), and their revenue base has shifted from India (35%) to NA (60%).

* The company\'s ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) is $80K, with average contract value increasing from $1,500 to $11,000-$12,000 due to new pricing models (platform fees + usage).

* Product-led growth: Focuses on inbound (60% of leads via content marketing and G2 rankings), outbound (30-40%), and some small experiments with paid ads (10%).

* Raised $450K previously and is planning to raise $2M to expand go-to-market activities and scale in the US. Expected ARR target is $1M post-fundraise.

**Key Challenges:**

* Competing with Merge.dev in the unified API space and others like API Deck and Combo.dev in Europe.

* Developing recurring revenue models and ensuring that larger customers stay with the platform long-term.

**Opportunities for Growth:**

* Potential to expand the business by selling not just to SaaS companies needing integrations but also to API providers who could offer Knit’s solution on top of their existing API documentation.

* Transitioning to a more product-driven, self-sustaining business model, focusing on big enterprise clients like HubSpot or Salesforce for higher contract values.

**Fundraising Strategy:**

* The company is still early-stage, seeking seed-stage funding. They need to show further traction with their new approach to attract Series A investment.

Financial Overview: - Projected year-end revenue: $16.1 million. - Slightly below the plan due to RV slowdown, but fundamentals are strong. - Opex better than planned, with 30% YoY growth and opex up only 8%, indicating operational leverage. 2. Market and Industry Analysis: - Macroeconomic view: Dealers carrying high inventory, potential industry challenges. - Believes in Rollick\'s approach through OEMs to support dealers during tough times. - Confidence inweathering the stormm with investor support and debt line. 4. Revenue and Growth Strategy: - Gross margin at 70%, up from 50%. - No churn on OEMs, low churn at dealers. - Intentional reduction of non-core tech revenue. - Targeting $20 million next yea, hoping to achieveg 10x forward revenue. 5. Exit Strategy: - Considering an exit in 12-14 months. - Likely buyer: A strategic entityPE ownsE for the product suite and customer relationships. - Prefers a strategic buyer over PE direct because the business is notg EBITDA-focused yet. 6. Cloverleaf.AI is a Software as a Service (SaaS) product that harnesses AI to analyze millions of hours of federal, state, and local government meetings. We utilize this data in two primary ways: risk mitigation and opportunity identification. Risk Mitigation: For instance, we were able to alert consumer food companies on April 18th about a growing ban on ingredients for various products, including Skittles. We provided subsequent updates on September 12 and alerted again when the bill passed on November 10. We are now reporting that New York and several other eastern states will likely follow suit in January. This makes us an indispensable tool for all regulated companies, especially enterprise. Opportunity Identification: In this aspect, we monitor discussions about potential spending, allowing us to keep a close watch on the $7 trillion spent annually on projects that bypass the RFP process. We specialize in various industries and assist companies, ranging from sidewalk firms to toll booth technologies, in staying informed about every local-level opportunity. This dual-product offering significantly expands our addressable market, valued at $7.9 billion. Please refer to our attached Market Analysis Assessment for detailed insights. Key Difference Citylitics relies on public documents to identify the previous infrastructure contract holders with cities or towns and their plans for upcoming large-scale projects. The vast majority of these projects go through the RFP process and require substantial investments in terms of time, energy, and resources from large companies. We differentiate ourselves through our data collection techniques, client interests (RFP vs. Non-RFP), and the scale of opportunities. We primarily cater to the SMB segment in infrastructure, while Citylitics focuses on major large infrastructure firms.Â Note: Beyond infrastructure, we can include firms such as Waste Connections and Waste Management in our scope. These companies operate city by city, and despite their large contracts, they typically circumvent the RFP process. We look forward to further discussions about a potential partnership.

Meeting with Ajay, Tariq, and Ravish. What do they do? They are involved in cyber risk modeling. In simple terms, cyber risk modeling means connecting three layers, namely the operational layer, functional layer, and enterprise layer, all together with one SaaS platform. They are aiming for a business model with 80% recurring revenue, 200% ARR growth starting this year, and 80% gross margin. 50% of the revenue and bookings will come through our channel partners. Strategic implementation partners include Capgemini (Singapore), PwC, and Wipro. They cater to the financials, retail, and manufacturing verticals with Capgemini, PwC in two areas (cyber and ESG) for family energy and utilities verticals, and Wipro in the cyber and ESG sides. Have they raised any capital so far? They have received $3 million in funding through convertible notes. The individuals from Fortune 500 serve as CXOs. What has been the revenue trajectory over the past few years? - 2020: $400K - $500K - 2021: $650K - $700K - 2022: $1.1M - 2023: Expected to be $2M to $2.5M (\"Sure thing\") - 2023 (Year-to-date): Approximately $750K They have a robust pipeline with active deal closures of 1-2 per month, with a new client signing a three-year contract worth $96K. Their sales strategy consists of 50% partnerships and 50% sales efforts. They participate in trade shows with Gartner and have a full-time director of sales. Their unique selling proposition (USP) lies in their use of AML risk modeling. They have over 300 models and approved patents for risk quantification using AML. How is the revenue split? - Product: 20% to 25% - Service: 20% - Consulting: 60% Product ARR is expected to account for 50% of the revenue. Their burn rate is $150K per month, and they have an 18-month runway before the series A funding. They are focused on achieving product-market fit. Their sales strategy includes the following approaches: 1. Convert proof of concept (POC) to annual recurring revenue (ARR). The sales cycle typically lasts 3-6 months, but they aim to reduce it to 3-4 months. 2. Land and expand: 20-25% of revenue comes from landing cyber deals, while the rest is generated through expansion. 3. Target specific niches, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A) and supply chain.

2013\| San Jose (United States)\| Seed

FlytBase is a pioneering technology company that provides an Internet of Drones (IoD) platform designed to automate and scale drone operations for enterprises. **Founded Year**: 2013  
  
**Location**: FlytBase is headquartered in **Pune, Maharashtra, India**, with additional operations in **Silicon Valley, California, USA**.  
  
**Team**:  
The company was co-founded by **Nitin Gupta**, who serves as the CEO. The team comprises experts in automation software, robotics, control systems, and machine intelligence.Market and Traction



* **Total Addressable Market (TAM)**: FlytBase targets the rapidly growing commercial drone market, which is increasingly leaning towards fully autonomous operations.

* **Traction**: The company has gained significant traction with a diverse customer base across North America, South America, Europe, Japan, Australia/New Zealand (ANZ), and Southeast Asia. It has been recognized for its innovation and has graduated from notable accelerator programs like Cisco LaunchPad.

Revenue and CustomersWhile specific revenue figures were not disclosed in the search results, FlytBase has reported having numerous enterprise customers globally.

**Ideal Customer Profile (ICP):**FlytBase primarily serves enterprises looking to leverage drone technology for operational efficiency. This includes sectors like logistics, construction, agriculture, and security.  
  
**Funding Stage and Investors:**  
Raised $1.5 million seed in 2019 from **Upekkha** and Cisco Launchpad  
  
**Nitin Gupta: Founder Overview**  
[https://www.linkedin.com/in/nitin7gupta][1]  
  
**Current Role**:  
Nitin Gupta is the **Co-Founder and CEO** of FlytBase. He has been instrumental in driving the company\'s vision of enabling drone autonomy for commercial applications.Background

* Nitin Gupta has a strong background in technology and entrepreneurship. He holds degrees from prestigious institutions including the **Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay** and the **University of Maryland, College Park**.

* Before founding FlytBase, he accumulated experience in automation software and robotics.

**Vision for FlytBase**  
Nitin\'s vision for FlytBase revolves around making drone operations accessible and efficient for enterprises by providing a modular and hardware-agnostic platform that integrates seamlessly with existing business applications.  
  
In summary, FlytBase is positioned as a leader in the drone automation space under Nitin Gupta\'s leadership, with a focus on delivering innovative solutions that cater to a wide range of industries.

**Company Overview and Focus:**

* Rockfish has a unique approach in the AI and data market, differentiating from competitors like Gretel, Mostly, and Hazy.

* The focus is on the evolving needs for AI LLM training and data management.

**Traction**

* Four contracted customers have new deals in the pipeline, including the Department of Homeland Security and Gilead.

* Several companies are in various stages of proof of concept (POC) and contracting, such as Toronto Dominion Bank, PNC Bank, and Deutsche Telekom.

* ARR achieved close to $3 million in total contract value and $1 million in ARR

**Use Cases and Solutions**

* Customers leverage operational data for AI model development, such as fraud detection, predictive maintenance, and anomaly detection.

* The company\'s value lies in bridging the gap between data and problem-solving, particularly in areas with sparse or limited data.



**Competitive Differentiation:**

* Competitors offer shallow models, requiring significant user effort.

* Rockfish provides a comprehensive, outcome-centric solution that integrates seamlessly with enterprise data.

Going

* spires to lead the \"third wave\" of synthetic data, focusing on democratizing technology and integrating it into every data ML pipeline.

* Envisions a copilot system to aid in the synthetic data needs of enterprises.

* Differentiating by offering comprehensive, easy-to-use solutions compared to competitors.

* Rockfish is establishing itself as a leader in synthetic data by providing a highly integrated and automated solution for enterprises.



Started with:

* initially engaged in collaborative consulting agreements with early design partners.

* transitioned to an automated platform approach, leveraging insights from early partnerships.

* Aim to automate 80% of the job, with a Copilot system assisting in refining configurations with customers.

**Product Focus**

* Emphasizes simplicity and automation in workflows, catering to diverse user personas, from data scientists to product owners.

* The platform automates model suggestions and data generation based on user configurations.



**Pricing Strategy**

* Pricing models include SaaS subscriptions tailored to specific use cases and enterprise deals targeting larger organizations with diverse data needs.

* Exploration of a startup package offering affordable options to early-stage companies.



**Market Dynamics and Use Cases**

* Increased awareness of AI capabilities, particularly generative AI.

From the CEO to Adhavan: Megh Computing is targeting the large and growing $8B intelligent video analytics market with its differentiated Video Analytics Solution (VAS). VAS is a fully customizable, cross-platform solution built on Open Analytics principles. Megh provides two offerings - VAS Suite of products and VAS SDK toolkit - that use video as a signal to create real-time insights for smart cities, smart factories, smart offices, and smart buildings. Meghâ€™s VAS platform is powered by the Nimble Application Framework for processing of data from cameras and sensors at the edge which allows customization across the entire pipeline for contextual analytics. Engineered to seamlessly leverage hardware acceleration for CPU, GPU, FPGA and SOC platforms, the framework makes VAS a truly high-performance, real-time analytics solution. Megh is seeing excellent traction for its VAS Suite with Managed Service Providers who provide security services. Megh\'s VAS SDK is getting adopted with System Integrators and Enterprises looking for a platform to provide customized solutions. Megh has doubled their revenue in 2021 to $800K establishing a successful pivot to providing end-to-end solutions. Megh is demonstrating a repeatable sales process driving over $1M in ARR. Megh is working with its channel partners to scale to over $2M in revenue in 2022. Megh has raised $7.5M in three seed rounds from Vulcan Capital, Rise of the Rest Fund, Rogue Venture Partners, Oregon Venture Fund and other investors. Megh is now finalizing the term sheet with a lead investor for a $8M Series A round. We would like to discuss the opportunity for you to join the syndicate for this round.

Adhavan\'s feedback: They fall under edge computing, specializing in video analytics. They don\'t do real-time analytics as in autonomous vehicles, but near-real-time applications like surveillance, smart buildings and apparently some defense contract in aviation. While I like their solution, not thrilled about pricing strategy, they license their SW, but have a recurring annual license component. They do have some impressive logos - Bosch, Walmart etc - with potential opportunities for expansion both as partners white labeling their solution as well as being their client.

**1 Meeting Details**

**Date:** 1st August  
**Time:** 11:30 – 12:30 PM IST  
**Attendees:**

* **Foster VC:** Priya

* **Simplicontract:** Makesh (Co-founder, Product Delivery & Customer Success)

* **DVC:** Dayakar, Varshnaya, Ashok

**2️ Company Overview**

* HQ: US-based with an India subsidiary

* Age: 5 years

* Investors: Kalaari (India subsidiary), Arka Ventures, Foster, Emergent, Picus Capital

* Funding: $4.7M raised (SAFE round) at $16M post-money valuation, money in the bank available

* Team:
  
  * Guru – CEO (ex-Microsoft)
  
  * CTO – ex-EY, led AI practice, second-time founder (previous startup \"Feel Easy\" failed post-Series A)
  
  * Makesh – ex-Biz Dev at Dynamics 365, now leading product delivery & customer success

**3️ Product Evolution**

1.  2019–2020: Initial focus on compliance in contracting

2.  2021: MVP launched, acquired Flipkart as first client

3.  2022: Pivot to Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM), mainly procurement contracts

4.  2024: Introduction of GenAI-powered \"Contract Intelligence (CI)\"
    
    * Proprietary NLP + 2–3 multi-layer agents to process unstructured contract data
    
    * Chunks documents for LLMs with audit trails
    
    * Addresses lawyer-specific language nuances
    
    * Privacy concerns minimal, adoption improving

**4️ Traction**

* Revenue:
  
  * 2022: $250K
  
  * 2023: $1.1M
  
  * 2024 (current): $1.8M
  
  * 2025 Target: $2.5M (CI: 2x growth, CLM: 1.5x growth)
* Key Deal: Reckitt ($1.2M over 3 years for CI, cold outreach)

* Pipeline: GSK ($700K/yr), Coca-Cola, P&G, Kaiser, HamGen (EPC sector), Zenoti (possible close)

* Customer Segments: Series B+ startups, CPG, pharma, EPC, healthcare, insurance

* ACV: $50K–$70K

* Go-to-Market: Startups (faster deal cycles), enterprise (longer cycles, bigger deals)

**5️ Market Opportunity**

* TAM: ~$50B (IDC), realistically ~$20B

* Problem: Contracts are largely unstructured data; existing solutions are services-heavy (Icertis, Coupa, Ariba, Conga, Apttus)

* Shift: Moving from point-in-time analytics (annual $500K–$700K spend) to real-time contract intelligence

* Value Proposition: Cost savings, revenue impact insights, tariff change implications for CFOs

**6️ Differentiation**

* Tech: Proprietary NLP + LLM agents, in-house data science team, enterprise knowledge graph architecture

* Category Creation: \"Contract Intelligence\" distinct from CLM wrappers

* Tailwinds: GenAI adoption in legal tech (previously slow to disrupt), model improvement accelerating value realization

* Microsoft Pegasus Program: Selected among 100 startups for agentic AI applications

**7️ Competitive Landscape**

* Direct Competitors: Icertis, Coupa, Ariba, Apttus, Conga

* Investor View: Icertis seen as disappointing (services-heavy, reliant on KPMG/BCG)

* Simplicontract Positioning:
  
  * Smaller, faster-moving than large players
  
  * True AI-driven approach vs services-first

**8️ Fundraising & Exit Outlook**

* Current Need: Potential round extension; aiming for $1M ARR in CI product alone by Dec 2024

* Long-term Exit: Foster in conversations with Thoma Bravo; target $10M ARR for strategic sale

**9️ Risks & Open Questions**

* Defensibility: Tech moat unclear long-term; pricing could be key differentiator

* Future of Space: Evolution beyond CI (e.g., voice, other contract interaction formats)

* Case Studies: Need strong client references (Reckitt, GSK) to prove repeatability

* Services vs Product: Large enterprises may still prefer services-led approach

**10️ Key Takeaways for DVC**

* Simplicontract is creating a new \"Contract Intelligence\" category with early traction in CPG and pharma.

* Proprietary NLP layer + LLM orchestration gives edge vs wrappers; however, moat is not fully defensible yet.

* Strong tailwinds: GenAI adoption, tariff implications, real-time intelligence demand.

* Potential opportunity for follow-on or extension round (favorable deal terms to be negotiated).

* Exit path likely via strategic buyer (e.g., Thoma Bravo) once ARR crosses $10M.

**Symmetry Systems**

Mon, 22 Dec 25

**Team**

* Mohit is the founder who can provide high-level company overview

* Company operates with pod-based structure across multiple locations:
  
  * Bay Area pod (where Mohit spent 3.5 years from 2020-2024)
  
  * Texas pod
  
  * Boston/DC area pod for East Coast GTM and DOD relationships
  
  * Italy pod with 4-5 senior engineers
  
  * India pod in Bangalore/Hyderabad with senior engineers
* Team focused on recruiting senior engineers who could build deep tech that “just works”

* Currently operates with median of 2 salespeople who are “the happiest salespeople on this planet” as their quotas are “long exhausted”

**Problem**

* Companies struggle with data security, particularly protecting sensitive PII data

* Large enterprises like UKG (Ultimate Kronos Group) handle extremely sensitive data including “Elon Musk’s PII” from customers like SpaceX, Tesla, Google, TSA

* These companies “can’t screw around with this problem” and need robust technical solutions

* Traditional approaches in data security space (DSPM) didn’t fully play out as expected

**Product**

* Data security platform that has evolved beyond original DSPM positioning into broader data security opportunity

* Platform handles multiple use cases across various environments

* Technology partnerships integrated with largest CSPMs (Cloud Security Posture Management platforms)

* Deep integration capabilities with compliance, automation, and storage companies for OEM partnerships

* Positioned as “deep tech thing that just works” as core priority

**Go-to-market**

* Heavily leveraged through delivery partners and channels including VARs, GSIs, and tech partners

* Plan to replicate successful Texas model across ~10 GEOs where they have marquee logos and teammates

* Strong presence in major industry events - participating in all CKO and SKO events for IN25

* Expansion strategy focuses on markets with existing marquee customer presence

* Direct sales motion supplemented by robust channel partnerships

**Traction**

* Currently at ~$7M ARR, expecting to hit $10M ARR in next few months primarily through Deloitte expansion alone

* Revenue growth trajectory: doubled every year for last two years, this year tripling (going from $2.5M to $7M)

* Major enterprise logos secured:
  
  * Deloitte Global (deployed across half the planet for multiple use cases)
  
  * UKG (Ultimate Kronos Group)
  
  * Won competitive POCs against Sentra, Cyra, and other major names
* 140% net dollar retention rate

* Zero voluntary churn to date (only losses due to companies going out of business or PE acquisitions)

* All current customers running AI security projects with the platform

* Committed ARR approaching total gross spend - near cash flow positive if not planning growth

* Strong pipeline with expansion opportunities already in progress and several marquee channel deals expected

**Funding**

* Total raised to date: $35M across three rounds
  
  * Seed: $3M
  
  * Series A: $15M at $60M post-money valuation
  
  * Safe note: $17M with $250M cap and 20% discount
* Currently raising Series B targeting $30M to reach $13M ARR in next 18 months

* Verbal indications suggesting $200-300M valuation range for Series B

* Safe note expected to convert at discount rather than cap given current climate

* Notable investors include CIO of Goldman Sachs and other prominent individuals who recently invested

* Goal is to reach $20M ARR, which could support $500M+ valuation based on comparable companies

* Citing [Security.ai][1] example: raised at $1B valuation with ~$20M ARR

* Operating philosophy: aim to get “within touching distance of default alive” at each round

**Agreed next steps**

* Ravish confirmed DVC won’t invest in safe note but would be interested in priced Series B round

* Mohit will check with colleagues and return with timeline and next steps

* Plan to reconnect in January after holiday break (people returning January 5th)

* Mohit will continue lead generation process and loop in DVC once terms start coalescing

* If room exists in Series B round and Mohit wants DVC to move quickly, sharing deck now would help with internal preparation and partner education

* Both parties agreed to wait until more certainty exists around round size and available allocation before formal process begins
